parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a member of the platform's airspace desk. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start your shift until you finish?
I don't know.
To help get us started, what is the very first thing you do when you sit down at the airspace desk in the morning?
I don't know.
Maybe it's easier to think about a specific memorable day—what was the worst day you've had at work in the last few months, and what made it so bad?
I don't know.
Who usually hands work to you during a shift, and who do you pass your work along to?
I don't know.
Is there any information or task you currently check by hand because you don't fully trust the existing tools or data?
I don't know.
When something goes wrong in the airspace or with a flight, what is the very first thing you need to know?
I don't know.
Thinking about a new software service being built for your desk, what are you most afraid it might get wrong?
I worry when closures are entered, because I want to know how much disruption was caused across customers. A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.
When a closure comes into force while drones are already in the air, how do you currently find out which customers and flights are disrupted?
I don't know.
What exactly do you need to know about the disruption across customers when a closure happens?
I want to know how much disruption the closure caused across customers. A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.
How do you measure or describe "how much disruption" a closure caused—for example, what specific numbers or details are you looking for?
I don't know.
Where do the airspace closures you enter come from, and who sends them to you?
I don't know.
What are all the steps you take when you enter a closure?
I don't know.
What happens right after you enter a closure—who needs to know about it, and what do you do next?
I don't know.
Besides entering closures, what other tasks do you handle at the airspace desk?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which is the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business, and I work for all customer companies with no business looking into any one company's operations. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
How do you set up or update the flight corridors between sites and the zones that group them?
I don't know.
When authorities announce a closure, does it apply to specific flight corridors, entire zones, or something else?
I don't know.
